prompt:
A densely annotated editorial infographic plate, drawn by hand in confident ink
line with light watercolour and gouache wash on bright warm-white paper.
Contour line varies in weight and is charcoal near-black. Dimensional but not
photographic: restrained hatching, subtle texture, believable volume, selective
shadow, clean uncluttered background. Every material reads as itself — dull grey
lead, unglazed earthenware, weathered timber, damp fibrous bark — and materials
that differ in the explanation look visibly different. Quiet palette of stone,
clay, wood, and metal tones over the warm-white ground, with one or two
desaturated accents that each keep a single meaning throughout the plate.
Contemporary editorial typography: one calm display face for the title, one
highly legible face for the many small labels, sentence case, crisply printed
and correctly spelled. Annotation is dense and disciplined — leader lines,
brackets, dimension marks, magnified inset circles, small side studies — laid
out so no two leaders cross. Asymmetric composition with about a quarter of the
page left quiet. Modern printing on clean stock: fresh, crisp, and unaged. The
only lettering anywhere on the plate is the title, the deck, the labels, and the
short notes. The words hero, drawing, figure, plate, inset, zone, band, strip,
trio, column, and cutaway describe the construction of the page and are never
lettered onto it, alone or in a phrase: no headings that name parts of the
layout, no percentages or
proportions of the page, no tags in brackets after a label or note, no sentence
describing the drawing or explaining what the reader is meant to see, no
signature, monogram, date, watermark, or credit line.

Title, set largest at the top left of the page: scaffold
Deck beneath it: A book's plan, written as tables, is dealt out into idea folders — one card and one sheet per essay — waiting for the mill to begin.

Hero: a planning table seen from above-left fills the upper middle. On it lies a large open plan document titled Plan for Math Book I, its visible page ruled as a table whose rows are readable as slim entries — a number, a short slug, a title, a phrase for the hook, a phrase for the hidden idea. Two sibling plans peek out beneath it, their edges labeled II and III, with a note: plans that share a name and differ by numeral are one series.

From the plan's rows, thin lines fan down and rightward to a carpenter's frame — an honest wooden scaffold of uprights and cross-pieces — on whose shelves finished pairs are set out in neat ranks: each pair is a written idea sheet and, clipped to it, a smaller filing card. One pair is enlarged in the middle right: the sheet shows a title, a paragraph headed the everyday experience and one headed the hidden math; the card behind it shows short ruled fields and a stamped word pending. A note at the pair: the sheet is for the writer, the card is for the machine; pending is the starting gun the pipeline waits for.

Two quiet details below:
- lower left: a small satchel labeled genre travelling from the plan table to the shelf, captioned — the series' genre — essay collection or novel — rides along and shapes the stubs;
- lower right: one shelf position already holding an older, hand-worn pair with a small hooked guard over it, captioned — an existing stub is never overwritten unless forced.

At the far right edge, a modest doorway with a conveyor leading through it, labeled: the pipeline collects from these shelves.

One warm accent colour follows the dealt pairs and the pending stamps; the plan, the scaffold frame, and the lines stay in ink.
